com: I saw another mighty Angel. Some expound it of Christ himself: others of an Angel, representing the power of God over the sea and land. (Witham)

Seven thunders uttered their voice, to signify the following approaching evils, which St. John is ordered not to write down, though they were shewn to him; and if he was not to write them, even in such a mystical and prophetical manner as he wrote the other things, who can pretend to know any thing of them? (Witham)

And when the seven thunders had, &c. St. John is not permitted to write, but ordered to seal up the things which the seven thunders had spoken; which circumstance seems to insinuate, that the things spoken by the seven thunders were seven particulars of antichrist’s persecution, as the word thunder is generally used in the Apocalypse to denote some disaster; and these seven particulars being most dreadful and severe, the Almighty chose to have them sealed up, or kept concealed, lest the foreknowledge of them should too much terrify and damp the human mind.

The Angel….swore….that time shall be no longer. This seems to favour very much the exposition of those interpreters who think that all these things are not to be fulfilled till some short time before the end of the world. Others (of which see Alcazar, &c.) take this to be a prediction of the ruin and destruction of the Jews, particularly under the emperor Adrian. Others (see the bishop of Meaux[Bossuet]) understand by this, that the time was approaching when God, by his judgments, would put an end to the idolatry and heathen worship of pagan Rome, and that his providence would make the Christian faith triumph over all its adversaries, and his Church flourish, as foretold by the ancient prophets; that is, this should come to pass when the seventh Angel should sound his trumpet. (Witham)

Declared. Literally, evangelized, to signify the good tidings, agreeable to the gospel, of the final victory of Christ, and of that eternal life which should be the reward of the temporal sufferings of the servants of God. (Challoner)

Take the book, and devour it. See Ezechiel ii. and iii. It was sweet in my mouth; I was delighted to read and hear the victories and glory of God’s faithful servants; but it became bitter in my belly, when I considered the judgments of God upon so many sinners, who by their own wilful blindness were lost for eternity. (Witham) — This mysterious book, presented to St. John precisely between the sound of the sixth and seventh trumpet, or rather between the irruption announced at the sound of the sixth trumpet, and the persecution which is then to follow and to precede the sound of the seventh trumpet, appears to represent the book of the gospel, which shall be given to the Jews at the end of the sixth age of the Church. This book will be then to them full of sweetness, because they will see in it the tender love of Jesus Christ; but at the same time it will cause bitterness, because they will see in it with grief their infidelity and that of their fathers. (Bible de Vence)
Thou must prophesy again: we may understand what still follows in this Apocalypse, or his gospel written afterwards, or his preaching and instructing the Asiatic Churches. (Witham)

Declared.... literally evangelized, to signify the good tidings, agreeable to the Gospel, of the final victory of Christ, and of that eternal life, which should be the reward of the temporal sufferings of the martyrs and faithful servants of God.
fa: Commentary on the Apocalypse of the Blessed John

"I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, clothed with a cloud; and a rainbow was upon his head, and his face was as it were the sun, and his feet as pillars of fire: and he had in his hand an open book: and he set his right foot upon the sea, and his left foot upon the earth. He signifies that that mighty angel who, he says, descended from heaven, clothed with a cloud, is our Lord, as we have above narrated. "His face was as it were the sun. That is, with respect to the resurrection. "Upon his head was a rainbow. He points to the judgment which is executed by Him, of shall be. …
The Chaplet, or De Corona
De Corona

The angel also, as he goes forth on a white horse, conquering and to conquer, receives a crown of victory; and another is adorned with an encircling rainbow (as it were in its fair colours)-a celestial meadow.
Commentary on Revelation

And I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, clothed with a cloud, and a rainbow on his head. Since above he had related the hardships of the Church, which it has suffered from heretics and pagans, it remains that he tell of its prosperity, how it has grown amid persecutions. For it is certain that the Church has grown in persecutions, and the more it was oppressed, the more it was strengthened and increased: as we read written about the children of Israel, in the figure of this same Church, that the more they were oppressed by the Egyptians, the more they multiplied. …
Commentary on Revelation

And his face was like the sun. The Lord is often signified by the sun, because the sun surpasses all visible creatures in its brightness and beauty; but what creature can be compared to its Creator? Yet through visible figures invisible realities are often shown. Therefore in the heart of the elect Christ is the sun, whom they never cease to behold by hope, and they believe that they will come to contemplate his beauty.
Commentary on Revelation

And his feet like pillars of fire. By the pillar of fire we can understand the Church, either because, inflamed by the Holy Spirit, it shines, or because it burns unceasingly with love of God and neighbor. By the two feet we must understand the two peoples. From the two feet, then, one pillar is formed, because from the two peoples, namely from Jews and Gentiles, one Church of God is built. We can also understand by the two feet the two Testaments, as we will show more fully in what follows. Nor does this disagree with the earlier meaning, since the Old Testament was delivered especially to the Jews, and the New to the Gentiles.
Commentary on Revelation

And he had in his hand a little book opened. This Book above is described as having been sealed with seven seals; but about its opening, by the Lord’s generosity, we have said some things. Therefore, our Lord Jesus Christ was seen holding the open little book in his hand, because he himself opened the meaning of the divine Scriptures for the teachers of the Church.
Commentary on Revelation

And he set his right foot upon the sea, but his left upon the land. By the right foot, as we have said, the New Testament is signified; by the left, the Old is indicated. We can, however, understand by the sea the people of the nations, on account of the depth of their ignorance and error; but by the land which is cultivated so that it may bear fruit, the Jews, who were cultivated through the discipline of the Law and bore fruit when they fulfilled the legal instructions, though in a carnal manner. …
Commentary on the Apocalypse of the Blessed John

"Seven thunders uttered their voices. The seven thunders uttering their voices signify, the Holy Spirit of sevenfold power, who through the prophets announced all things to come, and by His voice John gave his testimony in the world; but because he says that he was about to write the things which the thunders had uttered, that is, whatever things had been obscure in the announcements of the Old Testament; he is forbidden to write them, but he was charged to leave them sealed, because he is an apostle, nor was it fitting that the grace of the subsequent stage should be given in the first. …
Commentary on Revelation

And he cried out, as when a lion roars. Christ cried out through the Law, but not as when a lion roars; because in the one house of Israel his voice was heard only there. Afterwards he cried out through the Gospel, as when a lion roars; because his voice thundered forth into the whole world.
Commentary on Revelation

And when he had cried out, the seven thunders spoke their voices. By the seven thunders we can understand seven virtues. Christ cried out through the Law, but the seven thunders did not sound; he cried out through the Gospel, and the seven thunders spoke their voices. For those to whom the Law said, “Cursed is he who does not leave his offspring in Israel”; and for whom on this account it was permitted to have many wives and concubines, the thunder of chastity had not yet sounded. …
Commentary on Revelation

And I heard a voice from heaven saying to me: “Seal up what the seven thunders have spoken, and do not write them.” The voice from heaven is the voice from the Church; but to write is to preach, because just as a writer writes with ink in a scroll so that those who read may be trained, so too every teacher writes the words of God when, by preaching them, he plants them in the hearts of the listeners. Why then, by the voice that sounded from heaven, was it forbidden that the seven thunders be written, we can find in the Acts of the Apostles and in the letters of Paul. …
Commentary on Revelation

… When we swear, we want what we say to be firm. For the Lord, therefore, to have spoken is to have “sworn,” because it cannot come to pass that what God speaks should become void, just as he himself says in the Gospel: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Luke 21:33). Since Christ therefore swore by the One who lives forever and by him who made all creatures, he swore by himself, because all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made (Jn. 1:3). He swore, moreover, not by binding himself with certain words, but by speaking the things that were to come.
Commentary on Revelation

By the seventh angel, in fact, the preachers who are to be at the end of the world are signified, about whom we will speak in what follows. Christ therefore swore that in the days of the seventh angel the mystery of God will be completed, which he proclaimed through his prophets, because he foretold that the end will come then, when the full number of the elect has been fulfilled.
Commentary on Revelation

And the voice that I had heard from heaven spoke with me again and said: Go and take the book from the hand of the angel who is standing upon the sea and upon the land. He calls it the first voice, when it was said to him from heaven: Seal up the things which the seven thunders have spoken, and do not write them. (Rev. 10:4) Therefore he says that he heard the same voice again, because that voice was of the same Holy Spirit as this one. In this passage we must understand all the apostles through John. …
Commentary on Revelation

And he said to me: Take it and devour it, and it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet like honey. And when I had devoured it, my stomach was made bitter. By the mouth, in which tastes are distinguished, we can understand the hearts of the apostles; by the stomach, in which all the filth of the body stays, we must understand the memory of sins. Therefore, while the book was being devoured, it is said to have been sweet like honey; because when the divine Scripture is turned over in the mind and promises eternal life to those who keep the commandments of God, it becomes in the heart sweet as honey. …
Commentary on Revelation
And I went to the angel and told him to give me the book. The apostles went to Christ so that they might be instructed by him in the teaching of the divine Scriptures.
Commentary on the Apocalypse of the Blessed John

"I took the book from the hand of the angel, and ate it up." To take the book and eat it up, is, when exhibition of a thing is made to one, to commit it to memory. "And it was in my mouth as sweet as honey." To be sweet in the mouth is the reward of the preaching of the speaker, and is most pleasant to the hearers; but it is most bitter both to those that announce it, and to those that persevere in its commandments through suffering.
Commentary on the Apocalypse of the Blessed John

"And He says unto me, Thou must again prophesy to the peoples, and to the tongues, and to the nations, and to many kings. He says this, because when John said these things he was in the island of Patmos, condemned to the labour of the mines by Caesar Domitian. There, therefore, he saw the Apocalypse; and when grown old, he thought that he should at length receive his quittance by suffering, Domitian being killed, all his judgments were discharged. And John being dismissed from the mines, thus subsequently delivered the same Apocalypse which he had received from God. …
Commentary on Revelation

And he said to me: You must prophesy again to peoples, and nations, and tongues, and many kings. It is foretold to him that he will return from exile to preach. But since the holy Fathers hand down that after his return from exile he preached only in Ephesus and the places neighboring to it, and that there he died and his body rests, how is it said that he prophesied to peoples, and nations, and tongues, and many kings? …
ftr: John Litteral, released into the public domain
